title: Disinformation and Public Skepticism: Evaluating the Role of the Fake News on Trust in Pakistan Digital News Sphere
screen_reason: Online survey of 420 Pakistani digital-media users. Table 4 reports the distribution of self-reported exposure to fake news (Low 24.5%, Moderate 53.1%, High 22.4%), and Table 9 reports the share who say they have shared fake news without realising it (30.7%). Both are self-reported RECALL shares with an explicit denominator (N = 420), which §1 admits (a 'how often'/perceived-amount scale reported as a share of respondents above a threshold, and self-reported sharing).

estimates.country: Pakistan (respondents from Federal territory, Punjab, KPK, Sindh and Baluchistan)
estimates.platform: digital media generally (Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, WhatsApp, Twitter/X, online news websites)
estimates.date: not reported; article received 27 May 2025, published August 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents reporting a HIGH level of exposure to fake news
estimates.value_raw: Level of Exposure to Fake News: Low 103 (24.5%), Moderate 223 (53.1%), High 94 (22.4%) (Table 4, N = 420)
estimates.denominator: 420 Pakistani digital-media users aged 18+, recruited by non-probability purposive sampling through an online questionnaire
estimates.definition: Respondent placed in the 'High' category of a self-reported 'Level of Exposure to Fake News' measure; the underlying question wording and the cut-points for Low/Moderate/High are NOT reported in the paper
estimates.misinfo_def: no definition of fake news or disinformation is offered to respondents or stated in the methods; the paper uses 'fake news' and 'disinformation' interchangeably throughout
estimates.source_quote: The respondents were asked about their level of exposure to fake news. The majority of the respondents (53.1%) reported their exposure to fake news is moderate or normal, whereas 24.5% had low, and 22.4% had high exposure to fake news.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Table 4 (Effects of Being Exposed to Fake News on the Level of Trust), p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely self-reported on a closed-ended questionnaire (multiple choice, 5-point Likert and frequency items), piloted on 25 respondents; no item wording, no scale reliability, no weighting and no fieldwork dates are reported
estimates.moderator_quote: It involved a non-probability purposive sampling that guaranteed that the respondents are users of digital media. A survey of 420 respondents from age 18 onwards of diverse backgrounds (e.g., age, gender, education level, and region) was carried out.
estimates.notes: Recorded at the HIGH threshold only (94/420 = 22.4%). 'Moderate or higher' (75.5%) would be a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids, and the paper offers no 'never/none' category, so no 'share exposed at all' is derivable - an adjudicator should note the measure cannot produce the usual 'any exposure' figure. Confidence is LOW because the questionnaire item is never quoted, the Low/Moderate/High cut-points are undefined, and 'exposure' here may be perceived amount rather than a frequency of encounters. Sample is a non-probability online convenience/purposive sample skewed young (86% under 35), highly educated (87% bachelor's or above) and to Punjab/Federal (86%).

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have shared fake news without realising it
estimates.value_raw: Shared Fake News Without Realizing It: Yes 129 (30.7%), No 195 (46.4%), Not Sure 96 (22.9%) (Table 9, N = 420)
estimates.denominator: 420 Pakistani digital-media users aged 18+, recruited by non-probability purposive sampling through an online questionnaire
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'Yes' to whether they had shared fake news without realising it (alternatives: 'No', 'Not Sure'); no time window is specified
estimates.misinfo_def: no definition of fake news or disinformation is stated
estimates.source_quote: To see whether the respondents shared fake news unknowingly, they were questioned on whether they shared such fake news. The majority of respondents (46.4%) disagreed, 30.7% agreed, and 22.9% reported they are not sure whether they shared fake news unknowingly or not.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported, no verification against any behavioural or platform record; no item wording reported beyond the summary sentence; no time window
estimates.moderator_quote: The data was collected online through a structured questionnaire created on the basis of the given study... The questionnaire will be premised on closed-ended questions... Multiple-choice questions, Likert statements (1: Strongly Disagree- 5: Strongly Agree), and frequency statements (Often, Sometimes, Rarely, Never).
estimates.notes: A rare self-reported SHARING figure: 30.7% say yes, with a further 22.9% unsure, so the upper bound including 'not sure' would be 53.6% - that sum was NOT computed into the value (R8). The 'without realising it' framing makes this an unwitting-sharing measure (not intentional sharing), and no time window is given, so it is effectively lifetime. Same sampling weaknesses as the exposure row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Table 2 'Awareness of Fake News or Disinformation' (High/usually identify 182, 43.3%; Moderate/aware but sometimes unsure 223, 53.1%; Low/difficulty identifying 15, 3.6%) - NOT extracted: this is self-rated ABILITY to identify fake news, i.e. a discernment/confidence measure, which §1 excludes. (2) Table 9 'Platforms where People Encounter Fake News' (Facebook 48.6%, YouTube 18.1%, TikTok 13.3%, WhatsApp 6.4%, online news websites 4.8%, all of the above 4.8%, Twitter/X 4.0%) - NOT extracted: this is the attribution of WHERE respondents mostly encounter fake news, a single-choice platform distribution, not a share of respondents exposed on each platform, so it cannot be turned into per-platform prevalence rows. (3) Table 9 'Effect of Fake News on People's Opinion and Behavior' (Agree 94.0%) - a perceived-effects/third-person item, not exposure. (4) Table 6 verification behaviour (always verify 37.9%; never verify 1.2%; cross-check with news sources 49.0%) - coping behaviour, not misinformation prevalence. (5) 'Nearly 58 % of the Pakistani individuals think that the issue of fake news is a significant problem (Haque, 2017)' in the Introduction is cited from elsewhere and barred by R8. (6) The one-sample t-tests (awareness t(419) = 22.112; verification t(419) = 21.089) report mean differences on unnamed scales with no share attached. (7) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES that an adjudicator should see: Table 1 gives PhD and above as 12 respondents but '21.9%' while the text says 2.9% (12/420 = 2.9%); the text says 43.3% for the 18-24 age group while Table 1 says 44.3% (186/420 = 44.3%); and the figure 223 (53.1%) appears as both 'Moderate awareness' (Table 2) and 'Moderate exposure' (Table 4), which may be coincidence or a transcription error. The exposure and sharing tables I used are each internally consistent (103+223+94 = 420; 129+195+96 = 420).

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, non-probability purposive sampling of Pakistani digital-media users aged 18+; N = 420; structured closed-ended questionnaire (multiple choice, 1-5 Likert, frequency items) piloted on 25 respondents and reworded for comprehension; analysed in SPSS/Excel with descriptives, t-tests and linear regression; voluntary participation with informed consent and anonymity. NOT reported: fieldwork dates, recruitment channel, response or completion rate, item wordings, scale construction or reliability (no alpha), weighting, and how the Low/Moderate/High categories were derived. The sample is heavily skewed - 86.2% under 35, 86.7% with a bachelor's degree or higher, 86.2% from Punjab or the Federal area - so it is not representative of Pakistani internet users, let alone the population. The paper contains several arithmetic/typographical inconsistencies in its demographic table, and is published in a low-visibility multidisciplinary journal; treat both estimates as weak evidence.
